I loved Hacknet. It's short, the story's great, it's gripping, it's simple enough to get going yet difficult enough to engage and keep you playing. It's a brilliant evolution of games like Uplink, without all the damn clicking, and I can see it getting people to seriously consider learning to code.

Hacknet makes you feel like a virtual detective, without too much hand holding, giving you the tools you need to explore, then letting you run wild. Thoroughly recommended.

So I stumbled on this game pretty randomly, but as I read more about it here and on other sites reviewing games of its type, it piqued my interest. It seemed like it was pretty quick playthrough, and for $10 I though "What the heck? I give it a try".

After installing it and getting through the tutorial, I was hooked. I beat it in about 14 hours, but that was doing all but one mission, and taking plenty of time to dig around and read every little easter egg I found.

To explain my qualifications, I am not a programmer or hacker of any type, nor is either a requirement for this game. I can certainly find my way around a computer, and figure stuff out if something goes wrong (often with the help of the great and powerful Google), but I have very limited programming experience and have never (sucessfully) used Linux or any other UNIX system.

I cannot praise this game highly enough. I grew up in PC gaming, and still do a lot to this day. I'm not the "go out and buy the latest AAA title" gamer; I feel I strike a balance between enjoying some AAA titles, like Mass Effect, Assassin's Creed, etc, Indie games that some of my friends throw my way, and Classics like the Half Life series. This game was incredibly unique in it's execution, and forces you to learn to play it in a new way. Even for those familiar with UNIX, I'm not sure how many have used a UNIX command prompt as their primary UI in a game like this before. I was a little nervous at first, but the tutorial for the game gives you more than enough of an understanding to work with to start, and there's tips snuck in throughout the game to help remind you how to do things. If you ever forget, you have full and ongoing access to everything you've previously done for reference. The game gives you all the resources you need to solve the puzzles it presents while still offering an exciting challenge. If you do get stuck, there's plenty of support on Steam discussion boards to help you get passed whatever has you stumped.

This game apparently has a multiplayer option planned, which is supposed to drop after the Mac and Linux versions are stablized. I look forward to that very much.

Simply put, this game was a hell of a ride, and has ranked among my most enjoyable gaming experiences. The story isn't super long, but it's long enough to be incredibly enjoyable without ever really feeling repetitive (regularly a bane of modern AAA titles). If you have $10 and a few days to spare, it's defintely worth it for something unlike a lot of what most people are playing these days. Something different, expertly done.

Hacknet is an excellent hacking simulator. Its user interface is very convincing and sleek, and there is just enough recognizable computer-jargon to make it somewhat realistic without making it boring or too dense to understand. Using the command terminal is way faster (and way cooler) then just using the GUI and makes you feel like you're the real deal.

Downsides to the game are the occasional spelling mistakes and the lack of explanation at some points in the game. My biggest issue with the game, however, is the complete linearity of the game. It never feels like you're interacting with a bigger world around you, just a pre-determined set of servers you have to hack, which is a shame. If it could be expanded somewhat to include a more dynamic 'internet' for you to explore, and more leeway in how to approach missions, this would've been the new standard in hacking sims. As is, it's a great game, but Uplink still holds the title.

First of all, I never played Uplink, so I can't compare this to that. What I did play was the HackRUN saga, so please pardon my comparison to a not very similar game. I also think it's funny that there are .dll and .exe file on what is (seemingly) a Linux system, but I can ignore that.

In a nutshell, Hacknet is a hacking sim game with a decent storyline. That is something I don't see often. HackRUN also has a storyline, but it's pretty linear if you ask me. This game uses real UNIX commands. For those of you new to the coding world (I guess?), it won't be hard to pick up; the tutorial does a good job of introducing the commands, and the 'help' menu will always be there to help you. For those of you who are familiar with the UNIX command prompt, you will be pleasantly surprised. The animations you get when hacking is pretty cool too. The best part of this games\ is that there are some systems that will start tracing you once you start your hacks. You have 100 seconds to do whatever you need to do and GTFO the system, or else (I don't actually know what happens because I have never failed doing so). You can, disconnect midway to cut the trace short and come back in the system again to do your stuff (again) at a later time, but hey, where's the fun in that? Along the way of making yourself a name in the hacking world (in the game), you will encounter files that are seemingly unimportant (like IRC log files, random text files, etc.). You are half right, [b]most[/b] of these files are unimportant. They may contain jokes and the stupidity of internet friends chatting together; but the rest may contain passwords that will make your life much easier when attempting to access some systems or useful information on your target's location.

There are decent puzzles in this game that happens in a specific scenario, but the contracts you get are pretty repetitive: [spoiler]probe the system, bypass proxy/firewall if those are there, open some ports, hack in, do your stuff, clear logs, get out[/spoiler]. New commands are introduced every now and then, but those have instructions along with them, so it's pretty easy to do whatever you need to do after. Basically, it's not very challenging (unless the devs add a "No x-server" mode to force you to use the command prompt throughout the game, that would be really fun, devs pls read). The last thing that this game lacks is the ability to adjust the SFX volume. Me clicking things actually shocks me sometimes because trust me, the SFXs are loud.

In conclusion, Hacknet is a good hacking sim with a decent storyline and a bit of realism. Would I recommend? Yes. Would I play again? Yes.

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed this game. I like the Easter Egg finds and the different mission themes. But I personally feel that the developer holds my hand for a little too long, a little too much. For every tool I need, I’m told explicitly where to find it and how it’s to be used.  Given there isn’t a wide variety of tools at my disposal, it’s kind of a no-brainer and it feels formulaic soon enough. It does require more from the player towards the end. E.g. the clock mission and the impenetrable CCC stronghold. 

I believe the game would be more challenging and intense if 1) we were required to probe around more on our own, 2) we were given more stringent time constraints, 3) we were faced with larger, messier, and more varied file systems, 4) clues were more elusive, 5) we were hacked more often, and 6) there’d be dire consequences if we don’t wipe our tracks (Honestly speaking, I don’t wipe my tracks every single time. When it’s a 5-port hack, with proxy and firewall protections and time is running out, I’d think “Nah, just dc ...  dc  ... DC!!!!!! ..… “   I know it’s bad hacker practice, but then I also know nothing’s going to happen to me.) 

A not-to-be-missed game, especially when it’s on sale. At full price though, it’s a bit steep considering playtime is ~7 hours. Earnestly looking forward to the rumored multiplayer mode ….

Hacknet is certainly worth the $15 list price (and if it's on sale, even better).  The gameplay is highly atmospheric with an engaging storyline.  If you have a four or five hours to set aside, I'd recommend playing through in a single sitting - I did, and I found it made for a very immersive experience.  

The game does an excellent job of progressive puzzle solving.  I was reaching back trying to remember what tools and strategies I used in earlier hacks in my attempts to complete increasingly complex contracts.

On the downside, the hacking itself can get repetitive.  Around the 40th time I ran SSHCracker.exe, I found myself wishing I could just get to the next plot point in the story.  However, the game isn't too long, so the feeling of repetition doesn't turn into a feeling of grinding.  Additionally, the game progresses at a fast enough pace that it wasn't too long before I encountered a new type of defense or a new way to break into the system, and the "side quest" contracts are punctuated frequently enough by unqiue and highly engaging contracts.
